questions.question: Industries are classified into ___________ categories in the Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**three.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

 
• 
 
​Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR) 1956:-

 
 
• It laid the foundation for India’s second five-year plan and Industrial policy Resolution 1956, which paved the way for the development of the Public Sector and License Raj. 
 
• In accordance with the goal of the state controlling the commanding heights of the economy, the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 was adopted. 
 
• The 1956 Policy empha­sised the need to expand the public sector and build up a large and growing coop­erative sector. 
 
• It encourages the separation of ownership and management in private in­dustries and, above all, prevents the rise of pri­vate monopolies. 
 
• This resolution formed the basis of the Second Five Year Plan, the plan which tried to build the basis for a socialist pattern of society. 
 
• **This resolution classified Industries into three categories.**
 
• The first category comprised industries that would be exclusively owned by the government; the second category consisted of industries in which the private sector could supplement the efforts of the public sector. 
 
• It was based upon the Mahalanobis Model of growth which advocated that emphasis should be laid on the heavy industries, which can increase the economic output of the country. Mahalanobis model suggested the dominance of the heavy industries. 
 
• It laid emphasis on integrated infrastructure development as a prerequisite to private investment and therefore gave priority to power, transport, and financial institutions.
 
• It gave recognition to small-scale industries such as cottage industries with respect to balanced regional growth and also gave tax concessions and subsidies.
 
• It gave impetus to industrial development in far-off of the country to increase economic growth.
 
• It considered FDI as complementary to domestic growth provided a major share in control and management was to be given to Indian hands.

questions.question: Under the Industrial Policy Resolution 1956, industries in India have been classified into how many categories?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **__Three__.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Under the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956, industries were classified into three categories:** Schedule A, Schedule B, and Schedule C, **based on the level of government involvement in each sector.
 
• Industries under Schedule **A were considered critical for the national economy** and were reserved for the exclusive responsibility of the state. This included sectors like defense, atomic energy, and railways.
 
• Schedule **B industries were those where the state would play a dominant role**, but private sector participation was also allowed. Examples included chemicals, fertilizers, and machine tools.
 
• Industries under Schedule **C were left primarily to the private sector,** with the state stepping in only when necessary. This category included consumer goods industries.
 
• The 1956 Industrial Policy was a key document in laying the foundation for India’s socialist pattern of development, aiming for public sector dominance in key industries while allowing private participation in non-core sectors.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The IPR of 1956 was introduced in the backdrop of **India’s post-independence economic scenario**, focusing on industrial development and self-reliance.
 
• The policy was aligned with the goals of the **Second Five-Year Plan (1956-1961)**, which emphasized rapid industrialization through public sector investment.
 
• The IPR encouraged the establishment of Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) to operate in key industries and promote economic growth.
 
• Role of Planning Commission: The Planning Commission played a crucial role in formulating the IPR, and setting guidelines for industrial development.
 
• The policy introduced a licensing system for setting up industries, requiring businesses to obtain licenses to regulate entry and ensure compliance with government goals.
 
• The IPR imposed restrictions on foreign investment and technology transfer to promote domestic industries and protect local interests.
 
• The policy prioritized the development of **heavy industries, such as steel and machinery,** to support overall industrial growth.
 
• The IPR recognized the importance of small-scale industries and encouraged their development through **policies, loans, and financial support.**
 
• The Industrial Policy aimed to generate employment opportunities through industrial expansion and promote balanced regional development.
 
• The IPR of 1956 underwent several amendments and updates over the years, culminating in **new industrial policies in the 1980s and 1990s to liberalize and modernize the Indian economy.**

questions.question: What is the full form of ‘BPO’?

__
 
• The full form of BPO is **Business Process Outsourcing**.
 
• BPO involves contracting of specific business tasks, such as customer service or accounting, to a third-party service provider.
 
• It allows companies to focus on their core business functions and improve efficiency.
 
• BPO services can be categorized into back-office outsourcing, including internal business functions such as human resources or finance, and front-office outsourcing, which includes customer-related services such as contact center services.
 
• BPO can help businesses reduce costs, improve service quality, and access global talent.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• Involves subcontracting IT functions to external vendors, including software development, infrastructure management, and technical support.
 
• Helps businesses access specialized skills and technologies while reducing costs.
 
 
 
• **Knowledge Process Outsourcing (KPO)**
 
 
• Focuses on outsourcing knowledge-intensive tasks such as research, data analysis, and financial consultancy.
 
• Requires advanced analytical and technical skills to perform high-level processes.
 
 
 
• **Human Resource Outsourcing (HRO)**
 
 
• Involves contracting out human resources functions like recruitment, payroll, and employee training.
 
• Allows organizations to streamline their HR processes and focus on strategic HR activities.

• However, it is important to carefully regulate privatised sectors to ensure fair competition and prevent monopolistic practices.

questions.question: What gave a major impetus to the cotton textile industry in India after Independence?

__

• This movement fostered a sense of national pride and self-reliance among Indians, leading to increased demand and production of Indian goods.
 
• The Swadeshi movement laid the foundation for the growth of indigenous industries, which saw major development post-independence.

• The partition of India in 1947 led to the division of the country into India and Pakistan. While it had significant socio-political impacts, it did not directly give a major impetus to the cotton textile industry.

• During the British colonial period, India was a major exporter of raw cotton to England. However, this did not benefit the Indian cotton textile industry, as raw materials were sent to England for manufacturing finished goods.

• The development of the railway network in India did contribute to the overall industrial growth by improving transportation and connectivity. However, it was not the major driving force behind the cotton textile industry's growth post-independence.
 
 
 
• **Swadeshi Movement**
 
 
• The Swadeshi movement was a part of the Indian independence movement that encouraged the boycott of British products and the use of Indian-made goods.
 
• It significantly boosted the domestic cotton textile industry by increasing the demand for Indian textiles and reducing dependence on British imports.
 
• The movement also encouraged the establishment of new textile mills in India, leading to the growth of the industry.
 
• Post-independence, the momentum gained from the Swadeshi movement continued to support the development of the Indian cotton textile industry.

questions.question: Small scale industries in 1950 were defined as all those industries in which the maximum investment was ________ lakh rupees.
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In 1950, small scale industries were defined by the maximum investment limit in plant and machinery.
 
• The maximum investment limit for small scale industries was set at **five lakh rupees**.
 
• This definition was intended to encourage the growth and development of small scale industries in India.
 
• The investment limit has been revised multiple times over the years to keep up with inflation and economic changes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Small Scale Industries (SSI)**

 
 
• Small Scale Industries are industrial undertakings having a fixed investment in plant and machinery, whether held on an ownership basis or by lease or by hire purchase, not exceeding a prescribed limit.
 
• SSIs play a crucial role in the economic development of a country due to their contribution to employment, production, and exports.
 
• The investment ceiling for SSIs has been revised over the years to reflect changes in economic conditions and industrial growth.
 
• In 1950, the investment limit was set at Rs. 5 lakh, but this limit has been raised periodically to accommodate changes in the economy and inflation.
 
 
 
• **Evolution of SSI Definition**
 
 
• In 1950: The maximum investment limit was Rs. 5 lakh.
 
• In 1966: The investment limit was raised to Rs. 7.5 lakh.
 
• In 1985: The investment limit was further raised to Rs. 35 lakh.
 
• In 1991: The investment limit was raised to Rs. 60 lakh.
 
• In 2006: The Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises Development (MSMED) Act was enacted, which redefined the criteria for categorizing industries.
 
• As of now, the MSMED Act of 2006 classifies enterprises based on both investment in plant and machinery/equipment and annual turnover.
 
 
 
• **Importance of SSIs**
 
 
• SSIs are vital for economic growth as they provide large-scale employment and contribute significantly to GDP.
 
• They help in the utilization of local resources and promote balanced regional development.
 
• SSIs contribute to the export earnings of the country and help in the development of entrepreneurial skills among the population.
 
• They play a crucial role in the socio-economic development of the country by providing livelihood opportunities.

• The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 marked a significant step in India's economic planning by reserving certain industries exclusively for the public and private sectors.
 
• This policy aimed to accelerate industrialization and create a mixed economy where both public and private sectors would play pivotal roles.
 
• Under this resolution, industries were classified into three categories: Schedule A, Schedule B, and Schedule C.
 
• Schedule A included industries that would be exclusively owned by the State, Schedule B included industries where the State would play a dominant role, and Schedule C consisted of the remaining industries left to the private sector.
 
• The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 laid the foundation for the development of the heavy industries and infrastructure sectors in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Industrial Policy Resolution, 1948**

 
 
• This was the first major industrial policy statement by the Government of India after independence, which aimed to outline the role of the state in industrial development.
 
• It categorized industries into four broad areas based on state involvement and control.
 
 
 
• **Industries Development and Regulation Act, 1951**
 
 
• This Act provided the framework for the central government to regulate and control the establishment and functioning of industries in India.
 
• It aimed to ensure planned and coordinated development of industries across the country.
 
 
 
• **Statement of Industrial Policy, 1945**

questions.question: Which of the following industries was NOT in Schedule A of Industrial Policy 1956?

__
 
• **Mining of salt **was **NOT **in** Schedule A of Industrial Policy 1956.**
 
• Schedule A, consisting of **17 industries**, was exclusively under **the jurisdiction of the State**.
 
• Among these, **four industries arms and ammunition, atomic energy, railways, and air transport** were monopolized by the Central Government.
 
• **State Governments** were responsible for fostering the development of new units in the remaining industries.
 
• The industries listed in Schedule A were arms and ammunition and allied items of defence equipment, atomic energy, iron and steel, heavy castings and forgings of iron and steel, heavy plant and machinery required for iron and steel production, mining, machine tool manufacture, and other specified basic industries.
 
• Additionally, the schedule included heavy electrical plant, including large hydraulic and steam turbines, coal and lignite, mineral oils, mining of iron ore, manganese ore, chrome-ore, gypsum, sulphur, gold, and diamond, mining and processing of copper, lead, zinc, tin, molybdenum, and wolfram, minerals specified in the Schedule to the Atomic Energy (Control of Production and Use) Order, 1953, aircraft, air transport, railway transport, shipbuilding, telephones and telephone cables, telegraph and wireless apparatus (excluding radio receiving sets), and generation and distribution of electricity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956**, adopted by the Indian parliament in **April 1956,** marked a significant milestone in **India's industrial development strategy.**
 
• Following the **Industrial Policy of 1948**, it stood as the second comprehensive statement outlining the nation's industrial trajectory.
 
• Throughout subsequent** Five-Year Plans, the 1956** policy remained foundational, shaping India's economic landscape.
 
• Central to the resolution was the vision of establishing a socialist society, guiding social and economic policies towards this end.
 
• A key feature of IPR 1956 was the empowerment of governmental machinery, granting it enhanced authority in industrial matters.
 
• The resolution delineated three distinct categories of industries, each with its own delineated role:
 
 
• **Schedule A **encompassed industries deemed the exclusive responsibility of the state, highlighting the government's direct involvement and control.
 
• **Schedule B** identified sectors slated for progressive state ownership, where the government would establish new enterprises. Private enterprise was envisioned to supplement state efforts in these industries.
 
• **Schedule C** encompassed all remaining industries, where future development would predominantly be driven by private sector initiative and enterprise.

questions.question: The Industrial Policy Resolution, 1948 mainly categorised the large-scale industries into __________ fragments.

• This policy was the first comprehensive industrial policy statement by the Government of India, aiming to lay down the pattern of industrial development.
 
• The four categories were: industries with exclusive state monopoly, basic and strategic industries, industries requiring regulation and control, and other industries.
 
• This categorization was intended to balance the roles of the public and private sectors in the industrial development of the country.
 
• The resolution was a significant step in outlining the government's approach to industrial development in post-independence India.

• The Industrial Policy Resolution, 1948 aimed to promote a mixed economy where both public and private sectors would work together to achieve balanced industrial growth.
 
• It laid the foundation for subsequent industrial policies and was instrumental in shaping India's economic structure.
 
• The resolution also emphasized the importance of protecting small-scale industries and ensuring fair competition.
 
• It was followed by the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956, which further elaborated on the role of the public sector in industrial development.
 
• This policy framework was crucial in guiding India's industrial strategy during the early years of independence.

questions.question: What are the three components of the empowerment model in SAPAP of SHGs?

Social mobilisation, economic development, and education

• **Social mobilisation** refers to the process of bringing together all societal sectors to raise awareness, demand, and participation for the empowerment and development of Self-Help Groups (SHGs).
 
• **Capital formation** involves the accumulation of assets and investments to generate income and enhance the financial stability of SHGs.
 
• **Capacity building** focuses on enhancing the skills, knowledge, and abilities of SHG members to improve their organizational and operational efficiency.
 
• These three components together aim to strengthen SHGs, enabling them to become self-reliant and sustainable in their economic activities.

• SHGs are small, economically homogeneous affinity groups of rural poor, coming together to save and mutually contribute to a common fund.
 
• They provide members with support and resources to improve their living standards and economic conditions.
 
 
 
• **Microfinance**:
 
 
• It is a financial service for low-income individuals or those who do not have access to typical banking services.
 
• Microfinance includes loans, savings, insurance, and fund transfers to help the underprivileged.
 
 
 
• **Financial Inclusion**:
 
 
• It is the process of ensuring access to financial services and timely and adequate credit for vulnerable groups such as weaker sections and low-income groups at an affordable cost.
 
• Financial inclusion aims to connect people to the formal banking system to promote economic growth and development.
 
 
 
• **Livelihood Promotion**:
 
 
• It involves creating and enhancing opportunities for the poor to improve their income and employment prospects.
 
• Livelihood promotion includes training, skill development, and access to markets and financial services.
